newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG mercenaries would have caused atrocities -academic.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenaries would have caused atrocities -academic.

text.p: A failed plan by the Papua New Guinea government to use mercenaries to put down a secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island could have led to "an atrocity of the worst kind", an Australian academic said on Wednesday.
Professor James Griffin told a foreign affairs forum that the decision to employ British-based military consultancy Sandline International may have had a successful outcome but at a terrible cost.
"With the horrific weapons they had they might very well have been able to do it," Griffin said in an address to the Australian Institute of International Affairs.
"It would have been an atrocity of the worst kind."

Former Papua New Guinea Sir Julius Chan stood aside last month when military and civil protests erupted over the US$36 million Sandline contract to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

Griffin, who worked in the University of Papua New Guinea's history department from 1968 to 1990 and remains the university's emeritus professor of history, said Sandline's 70 African mercenaries would probably have defeated the Bougainville Revolutuionary Army (BRA) rebels.
Instead the mercenaries were escorted out of the country by troops loyal to former army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who was sacked by Chan after he demanded Chan resign over the contract.
Griffin said the mercenaries would have had superior firepower to the BRA rebels, whom he described as guerillas.
Sandline's weaponry included two helicopter gunships, two transport helicopters, military vehicles, assault rifles, about 500 cases of ammunition and explosives, rockets and heat-seeking missiles.
But the arsenal never reached the mercenaries and was instead diverted to an airforce base in northern Australia after Chan and two senior ministers stood aside.
"They would have, with their de-oxygenating fuel-air bombs and so on, simply blasted away the village that stood in their way," Griffin said.
"The harder they were pushed by the BRA, the more likely they were to indulge in atrocities of that kind."
